paragraphs: “Thank goodness he didn’t ask me about Grushenka,” thought Alyosha as he left his father’s house and headed for Madame Hohlakov’s. “Otherwise I might have had to tell him I met Grushenka yesterday.”

Alyosha felt painfully that since yesterday both of the rivals had found new strength, and their hearts had hardened again. “Father is spiteful and angry. He’s made some plan and he’ll stick to it. And what about Dmitri? He’ll be harder than he was yesterday too. He must be spiteful and angry as well, and no doubt he’s made a plan of his own. Oh, I must find him today, whatever happens.”

But Alyosha didn’t have long to brood. Something happened on the road that seemed trivial, yet it made a deep impression on him. He had just crossed the square and turned the corner into Mihailovsky Street, which is cut off from the High Street by a small ditch (our whole town is crisscrossed with ditches). At the bridge he saw a group of schoolboys between nine and twelve years old. They were on their way home from school. Some had their bags on their shoulders, others had leather satchels slung across their chests. Some wore short jackets, others little overcoats. A few even had those high boots, creased around the ankles, that little boys spoiled by rich fathers love to wear. The whole group was talking eagerly about something, apparently holding a council. Ever since his Moscow days Alyosha had never been able to walk past children without noticing them. He was fondest of children around three, but he liked schoolboys of ten and eleven too. So, anxious as he was today, he wanted to turn aside at once and talk to them. He looked into their excited, rosy faces and saw right away that every boy had a stone in his hand. On the other side of the ditch, about thirty paces off, another schoolboy was standing by a fence. He also had a satchel at his side. He was about ten years old, pale and delicate-looking, with sparkling black eyes. He was watching the other six closely and anxiously. They were clearly his schoolmates, he had just come out of school with them, but he had obviously had a quarrel with them.
Alyosha went up to a fair, curly-headed, rosy boy in a black jacket and remarked:
“When I used to carry a satchel like yours, I always wore it on my left side, so that my right hand would be free. You’ve got yours on the right. It’ll be awkward for you to get at it.”

Alyosha had no craft or calculation in opening with this practical remark. But it is the only way for a grown-up to win a child’s confidence at once, and even more so a group of children. You have to begin in a serious, businesslike way, so that you stand on a perfectly equal footing. Alyosha understood this by instinct.
“But he’s left-handed,” answered another boy at once, a fine, healthy-looking boy of eleven. All the others stared at Alyosha.
“He even throws stones with his left hand,” said a third.
At that moment a stone flew into the group. It only just grazed the left-handed boy, though it had been thrown well and hard by the boy on the other side of the ditch.

“Give it to him, hit him back, Smurov!” they all shouted. But Smurov, the left-handed boy, needed no urging. He got his revenge at once and threw a stone, but it missed the boy and hit the ground. The boy on the other side of the ditch, whose coat pocket was plainly bulging with stones, flung another at the group. This time it flew straight at Alyosha and hit him painfully on the shoulder.

“He aimed it at you, he meant it for you. You’re Karamazov, Karamazov!” the boys shouted, laughing. “Come on, all throw at him at once!” Six stones flew at the boy. One hit him on the head and he fell down, but he leapt up again at once and began to fire back furiously. Both sides threw stones without stopping. Many in the group had their pockets full too.
“What are you doing! Aren’t you ashamed? Six against one! Why, you’ll kill him,” cried Alyosha.
He ran forward and stood in the way of the flying stones to shield the lone boy. Three or four of them stopped throwing for a minute.

“He started it!” cried a boy in a red shirt, in an angry childish voice. “He’s a beast. The other day in class he stabbed Krassotkin with a penknife. It bled. Krassotkin wouldn’t tell on him, but he has to be thrashed.”
“But what for? I suppose you tease him.”

“There, he sent a stone into your back again, he knows who you are,” cried the children. “It’s you he’s throwing at now, not us. Come on, all of you, at him again, don’t miss, Smurov!” And again a hail of stones began, a vicious one. The boy on the other side of the ditch was hit in the chest. He screamed, started to cry and ran away uphill toward Mihailovsky Street. They all shouted: “Aha, he’s scared, he’s running away. Wisp of tow!”
“You don’t know what a beast he is, Karamazov. Killing is too good for him,” said the boy in the jacket, his eyes flashing. He seemed to be the eldest.
“What’s wrong with him?” asked Alyosha. “Is he a tattletale or what?”
The boys looked at one another as though in mockery.
“Are you going that way, to Mihailovsky?” the same boy went on. “Catch up with him.... You see, he’s stopped again. He’s waiting and looking at you.”
“He’s looking at you,” the other boys chimed in.
“Ask him whether he likes a disheveled wisp of tow. Do you hear? Ask him that!”
They all burst out laughing. Alyosha looked at them, and they looked back at him.
“Don’t go near him, he’ll hurt you,” Smurov cried in a warning voice.
“I won’t ask him about the wisp of tow, because I expect you tease him with that question somehow. But I’ll find out from him why you hate him so much.”
“Go on and find out, then,” cried the boys, laughing.
Alyosha crossed the bridge and walked uphill along the fence, straight toward the boy.
“You’d better watch out,” the boys called after him. “He’s not afraid of you. He’ll stab you in a minute, on the sly, the way he did Krassotkin.”

The boy waited for him without moving. As Alyosha came up, he saw a child of about nine standing in front of him. He was small and weak, with a thin, pale face and large dark eyes that stared at him with spite. He was wearing a shabby old overcoat that he had grown out of far too much. His bare arms stuck out past the sleeves. There was a big patch on the right knee of his trousers, and in his right boot, right at the toe, there was a big hole in the leather, carefully blackened with ink. Both pockets of his coat were weighed down with stones. Alyosha stopped two steps in front of him and looked at him questioningly. The boy saw at once from Alyosha’s eyes that he wasn’t going to hit him. He grew less defiant and spoke first.
“I’m alone, and there are six of them. I’ll beat them all, alone!” he said suddenly, his eyes flashing.
“I think one of the stones must have hurt you badly,” remarked Alyosha.
“But I hit Smurov on the head!” cried the boy.
“They told me you know me, and that you threw a stone at me on purpose,” said Alyosha.
The boy looked at him darkly.
“I don’t know you. Do you know me?” Alyosha went on.
“Leave me alone!” the boy cried irritably. But he didn’t move, as if he were waiting for something, and again there was a spiteful light in his eyes.
“All right, I’m going,” said Alyosha. “Only I don’t know you, and I don’t tease you. They told me how they tease you, but I don’t want to tease you. Good-by!”

“Monk in silk trousers!” cried the boy, following Alyosha with the same spiteful, defiant look. He threw himself into a defensive stance, sure that Alyosha would now fall on him. But Alyosha turned, looked at him and walked away. He hadn’t gone three steps before the biggest stone the boy had in his pocket hit him painfully in the back.

“So you’ll hit a man from behind! They’re telling the truth, then, when they say you attack on the sly,” said Alyosha, turning around again. This time the boy hurled a stone savagely straight at Alyosha’s face. But Alyosha had just enough time to guard himself, and the stone struck him on the elbow.
“Aren’t you ashamed? What have I done to you?” he cried.

The boy waited in silent defiance, certain that Alyosha would attack him now. Seeing that even now he wouldn’t, he flew into a rage like a little wild beast’s. He rushed at Alyosha himself, and before Alyosha had time to move, the spiteful child had seized his left hand in both of his and bitten his middle finger. He sank his teeth into it and it was ten seconds before he let go. Alyosha cried out with pain and pulled his finger away with all his might. At last the child let go and backed off to his former distance. Alyosha’s finger had been bitten badly, to the bone, close to the nail, and it began to bleed. Alyosha took out his handkerchief and bound it tightly around his injured hand. It took him a full minute to bandage it. The boy stood waiting the whole time. At last Alyosha raised his gentle eyes and looked at him.
“All right,” he said, “you can see how badly you’ve bitten me. That’s enough, isn’t it? Now tell me, what have I done to you?”
The boy stared in amazement.

“I don’t know you, and it’s the first time I’ve seen you,” Alyosha went on, with the same calm, “but I must have done something to you. You wouldn’t have hurt me like this for nothing. So what have I done? How have I wronged you? Tell me.”

Instead of answering, the boy burst into a loud, tearful wail and ran away. Alyosha walked slowly after him toward Mihailovsky Street. For a long time he could see the child in the distance, still running as fast as ever, without turning his head, and no doubt still wailing in tears. Alyosha made up his mind to find him as soon as he had time and to solve this mystery. Just now he had no time.
